name: Ion diode
description: An ion diode turned inside out: the ring is the cathode, emitting electrons from its inner face, and the rod in its middle, on your supply, emits ions. Without a magnetic field the electrons rush to the rod and waste the supply's current. Your solenoid (the yellow coil, top right) curls them: above Hull's critical field they cannot reach the rod, and stay in a sheath along the ring. The heavy ions still cross, and the sheath's negative charge pulls more of them across. Deliver an ion current between 5 and 8.5 to the ring while at most 0.05 of electrons leak to the rod (averaged over $t = 20$ to $30$). The critical field grows with the voltage, as $B \propto \sqrt{V}$: too weak a field for your voltage lets the electrons leak; the sheath helps the ions most just above it. The thin outer ring is the tube's grounded envelope.

reality.represents: A magnetically insulated ion diode, as in pulsed-power ion sources

remarks.detail: Hull's cutoff for the heavy ions is 18 times the electrons', so a field that holds the electrons in a sheath lets the ions cross, and the sheath's charge draws more of them.
The electron sheath keeps spreading towards the anode, as in real ion diodes (their impedance collapse): the goal's window is a fixed time after switch-on.
Real magnetically insulated diodes run on pulsed power, megavolts for tens of nanoseconds; here a steady supply.

The ions are 16 times heavier per charge than the electrons, not 1836 times or more: in a static field the mass changes neither the paths nor the electrons' gain, only the time scale and the ion current (√(m_e/m_i) of the electrons' in a planar diode).

The tube is the same all along its length: its electrodes are long prisms, its electrons long lines of charge, its currents per unit length. A real tube is a few centimetres long and has end effects; the textbooks' planar and coaxial laws assume this symmetry too.
